title: PagedAttention and prefix caching
summary: How vLLM stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks behind per-request block tables, shares blocks with copy-on-write, and reuses cached prefixes via chained block hashes or SGLang's radix tree.
outcomes: Explain why contiguous max-length KV allocation wastes memory and limits batch size
Trace how a block table maps logical KV blocks to physical blocks during prefill and decode
Compute memory saved by sharing prompt blocks with reference counts and copy-on-write
Predict which prompt tokens hit vLLM's prefix cache using chained block hashes and LRU eviction
Compare RadixAttention with hash-based caching and judge when prefix caching pays off

lessons.title: Why contiguous KV allocation wastes most of the memory

blocks.md:
Recall from the KV cache course: during decoding, every token's key and value vectors are kept in GPU memory so later tokens can attend to them without recomputing them. Serving throughput depends on how many requests you can batch, and the batch size is capped by how many KV caches fit in memory at once.

The vLLM paper (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023) measured a 13B-parameter model on a 40 GB NVIDIA A100: about 65% of memory holds the weights, which never change, and close to 30% holds the KV cache. So the way the KV cache is managed decides the batch size.

blocks.caption: KV cache per token for OPT-13B, the paper's own example. At the model's 2048-token maximum, one request can need about 1.68 GB.

blocks.md:
In the paper's setup (Table 1), OPT-13B on one A100 leaves 12 GB for the KV cache, which is about 15,728 token slots. Systems before vLLM, such as FasterTransformer and Orca, stored each request's KV cache as one *contiguous* tensor, because most deep learning kernels expect contiguous memory. Since nobody knows in advance how long the output will be, they reserved a chunk sized for the request's maximum possible length.

The paper names three kinds of waste that follow from this:

- **Reserved** slots: held for tokens that will be generated later, so nobody else can use them now.
- **Internal fragmentation**: slots inside the chunk that are never used because the request stopped early.
- **External fragmentation**: free gaps between chunks that are too small for the next request.

blocks.title: Contiguous reservation in a 24-slot toy memory

scenes.caption: Request A arrives with a 7-token prompt and a maximum length of 12. The allocator reserves 12 contiguous slots: 7 hold prompt KV, 5 sit reserved for future tokens.
Request B (4-token prompt, maximum 8) gets slots 14 to 21. Slots 12 and 13 stay free: a gap left by an earlier request.
Request C needs 4 contiguous slots. Four slots are free (12, 13, 22, 23) but no 4 of them are adjacent, so C must wait. That is external fragmentation.
A decodes two tokens into its reserved slots. B emits end-of-sequence after 6 tokens, so slots 20 and 21 were never used: internal fragmentation. Only 15 of 24 slots hold real token states.

blocks.title: Share of KV memory holding actual token states

scenes.caption: Measured in the vLLM paper (Fig. 2). Orca variants reserve the model maximum, up to 2x the true output, or exactly the true output (an impossible oracle). Even the oracle wastes most memory to fragmentation.

blocks.prompt: Simplified model: 15.7K slots, every request reserves the 2048-token maximum, versus an allocator that only spends what a request actually uses. ShareGPT requests (shared ChatGPT chats) in the paper average about 499 tokens (input plus output). Roughly how many requests fit in each case?
blocks.reveal:
Contiguous at maximum length: 15,728 / 2048 = **7** requests. Allocating only what is used, with at most a few slots of slack each: about 15,728 / 507 = **31** requests, over 4x more.

This back-of-the-envelope estimate ignores that live requests are only partly grown, but it lands near the paper's measurement: vLLM batched 4.3x more requests than Orca (Max) on OPT-13B with ShareGPT.

blocks.md: Decoding is memory-bound, so throughput comes from batch size, and batch size comes from how many KV caches fit. Any slot that is reserved, fragmented, or duplicated is a request you could not batch.

Knowing the exact output length would not fix this. Orca (Oracle) assumes perfect knowledge and still stores real token states in only 38.2% of KV memory, because contiguous chunks of different sizes still fragment the space and still cannot be shared.

blocks.question: A request reserves 2048 contiguous slots and finishes after 300 tokens. What kind of waste are the 1748 untouched slots?
options: External fragmentation, because they sit between other requests
Internal fragmentation, because they are inside the request's own chunk and were never used
Reserved slots, because they will be used by later tokens of the same request
No waste, because the allocator frees them when the request ends
blocks.explain: They are inside the request's allocation and were never filled, which is internal fragmentation. The paper notes it is only known to be waste after the request finishes. Reserved slots are the ones that will eventually be filled; external fragmentation is space between allocations.

blocks.question: Which change would most increase batch size for a contiguous-allocation server?
options: Use a faster attention kernel
Increase the maximum sequence length so fewer requests are rejected
Allocate KV memory in small fixed-size pieces on demand instead of one max-length chunk per request
Sort waiting requests by prompt length before batching them
blocks.explain: Waste comes from reserving for the worst case in one contiguous piece. Allocating small fixed-size pieces only when tokens arrive removes reservation and external fragmentation and caps internal fragmentation at one piece per sequence. That is exactly PagedAttention's design.

lessons.title: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache

blocks.md:
PagedAttention borrows the operating system's answer to fragmentation: **paging**. The paper's analogy is direct: KV blocks are pages, tokens are bytes, and requests are processes.

A **KV block** holds the keys and values of a fixed number of tokens, the **block size** $B$. A request sees its KV cache as a list of *logical* blocks, filled left to right. A per-request **block table** maps each logical block to a *physical* block anywhere in a pool that the engine carves out of GPU memory at startup. Each entry also records how many slots are filled.

scenes.caption: Prefill of request A, prompt "Four score and seven years ago our" (7 tokens). Only 2 blocks are allocated, not the maximum length: logical 0 maps to physical 7, logical 1 to physical 1. Logical 1 has one free slot.
First decode step: the new token "fathers" goes into the free slot of logical block 1. No allocation happens; only the filled count changes.
Second decode step: logical block 1 is full, so the manager grabs any free physical block (here 3) for logical block 2. Logically contiguous, physically scattered.
A second request B with a 6-token prompt gets physical blocks 5 and 2. Both requests share one pool; each wastes at most the unfilled tail of its last block.

blocks.md: Request A's first three scenes follow Fig. 6 of the paper. Because a new physical block is allocated only when the previous one is full, the waste per sequence is bounded by one partly filled block. Every block has the same size, so there is no external fragmentation: any free block fits any request.

blocks.title: Translating a token position to a physical slot
blocks.code:
B = 4                   # tokens per block
table = [7, 1, 3]       # request A: entry i = physical block of logical block i

def slot(pos):
    blk, off = divmod(pos, B)
    return table[blk] * B + off

for pos in [0, 5, 8]:
    print(pos, slot(pos))

scenes.caption: Position 0 is in logical block 0, offset 0. The table sends it to physical block 7, slot 28 of the pool.
Position 5 ("ago") is logical block 1, offset 1. Physical block 1 starts at slot 4, so the slot is 5.
Position 8 ("brought") is logical block 2, offset 0, which lives in physical block 3: slot 12. The kernel does this lookup on the fly.

blocks.md: Attention itself is rewritten block by block. With key block $K_j$ and value block $V_j$ holding tokens $(j-1)B+1$ to $jB$, the query of token $i$ is scored against one block at a time, wherever that block lives:

blocks.tex: A_{ij}=\frac{\exp\left(q_i^\top K_j/\sqrt{d}\right)}{\sum_{t=1}^{\lceil i/B\rceil}\exp\left(q_i^\top K_t\mathbf{1}/\sqrt{d}\right)},\qquad o_i=\sum_{j=1}^{\lceil i/B\rceil} V_j A_{ij}^\top
blocks.caption: Eq. 4 of the vLLM paper. The result is exactly the same as ordinary attention; only the memory access pattern changes.

blocks.title: Expected KV waste per sequence: paged vs reserve-max

scenes.caption: Simplified model: the last block is on average half empty, about (B-1)/2 slots. With B = 16 a 500-token sequence wastes about 1.5%, while reserving 2048 slots wastes 76%.
With B = 128 short sequences waste much more: the paper saw large blocks hurt on Alpaca, whose sequences are often shorter than one block.
B = 1 wastes nothing but forces the kernel to fetch one token at a time. The paper found 16 large enough for GPU efficiency and small enough for low waste, and made it vLLM's default.

blocks.md: The block table is the whole trick: contiguous logical blocks, scattered physical blocks, allocation on demand. Waste is capped at one partly filled block per sequence.

Paging is not free. The paper measured 20 to 26% higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer's kernel, from block-table lookups, extra branches and variable lengths. It still wins end to end because only the attention operator pays, and the larger batch more than makes up for it.

blocks.question: A kernel reads the KV of position `pos` at `base + pos * bytes_per_token`, as a contiguous kernel would. After switching to paged storage, what goes wrong?
options: It reads the right tokens only while the sequence fits in its first block; later positions land in whatever block happens to sit next in memory
Nothing, because physical blocks are allocated in increasing order
It reads correct data but more slowly
It fails only for requests that share blocks
blocks.explain: Logical blocks are mapped to arbitrary physical blocks (7, 1, 3 in the example). Only offsets inside a block are contiguous, so every access must go through the block table: `table[pos // B] * B + pos % B`.

blocks.question: Why does vLLM avoid a block size of 1 even though it minimizes wasted slots?
options: Block tables cannot store more than 1024 entries
Copy-on-write needs at least two tokens per block
Prefix caching only works with block sizes that are powers of two
The kernel processes fewer positions in parallel per fetch, underusing the GPU
blocks.explain: The paper explains that more tokens per block let the PagedAttention kernel process more positions in parallel. Too small underuses the GPU, too large raises internal fragmentation and lowers sharing. 16 was the default it chose.

lessons.title: Sharing blocks with reference counts and copy-on-write

blocks.md:
Paging also makes **sharing** cheap. In *parallel sampling* one prompt produces several outputs, so every output sequence starts with the same prompt KV. With a block table, two sequences can simply point their logical blocks at the same physical blocks.

To know when a shared block can be freed or modified, each physical block keeps a **reference count**: how many logical blocks map to it. vLLM borrows **copy-on-write** from OS process forking: a block with a count above 1 is copied before anyone writes into it.

blocks.title: Parallel sampling: share the prompt, copy on write

scenes.caption: Prefill runs once for the shared prompt. Both samples map logical blocks 0 and 1 to physical blocks 7 and 1, so each has reference count 2. One copy of the prompt KV serves both.
A1 samples "fathers" and must write it into its logical block 1. That physical block is shared (ref 2), so writing in place would corrupt A2's context.
Copy-on-write: allocate physical 3, copy block 1 into it, point A1 at it, and drop block 1's count to 1. A1 then writes "fathers" into its private copy.
A2 samples "mothers". Block 1 now has count 1, so A2 writes in place with no copy. Only the last, partly filled prompt block was ever duplicated.

blocks.prompt: A request asks for 4 samples of a 100-token prompt, each generating 50 tokens, with block size 16. How many blocks are needed without sharing, and with prompt sharing plus copy-on-write?
blocks.reveal:
Without sharing: each sequence has 150 tokens, so ceil(150/16) = 10 blocks, times 4 = **40**.

With sharing: the 6 full prompt blocks (96 tokens) are stored once. Each sample then owns its remaining 54 tokens (4 prompt tokens in the copied last block plus 50 new ones): ceil(54/16) = 4 blocks each. Total 6 + 4 x 4 = **22**, a 45% saving.

blocks.md:
**Beam search** shares even more. Beam candidates share the prompt and often long stretches of generated text, and the sharing pattern changes every step as candidates are dropped and forked, like a process tree. When a candidate is dropped, vLLM decrements the counts of its blocks and frees any that reach 0. Older systems had to copy large parts of one candidate's KV into another; vLLM copies at most one block.

Internally the engine supports all of these with three operations on sequences: `fork`, `append` and `free`.

scenes.caption: Low end of the ranges in the paper (blocks saved by sharing divided by blocks needed without sharing), across numbers of samples or beam widths.
High end of the ranges. Beam search saves far more because candidates share generated tokens too, and ShareGPT's longer prompts make sharing pay more.

blocks.md:
**When memory runs out.** Requests grow one block at a time, so the pool can fill mid-generation. vLLM schedules first come, first served and preempts the latest arrivals first. Since a sequence needs all its blocks to make progress, eviction is *all or nothing* per sequence (and per group of sequences that share blocks). The evicted KV is then recovered in one of two ways:

- **Swapping**: copy the blocks to CPU memory and back later.
- **Recomputation**: drop them and rerun prefill on prompt plus generated tokens in one pass, which is much faster than the original token-by-token decode.

The paper found swapping costly with small blocks, because each block becomes a tiny PCIe transfer, and recomputation's cost independent of block size. For block sizes from 16 to 64 the two performed comparably end to end.
A physical block may back many logical blocks. Reference counts say when it can be freed; copy-on-write makes writes into shared blocks safe, at the cost of copying one block.

blocks.question: Two samples share physical block 9 (ref 2) as their last prompt block. Sample 1 writes first, then sample 2. How many block copies happen?
options: Two, one per sample
One: sample 1 copies, which leaves block 9 with ref 1, so sample 2 writes in place
Zero, because writes to the last block are always private
One, but sample 2 makes it because it writes second
blocks.explain: Copy-on-write triggers only when the count is above 1. Sample 1 sees ref 2, copies into a new block and decrements block 9 to 1. Sample 2 then owns block 9 alone and writes in place, exactly as in the paper's Fig. 8.

blocks.question: Why does vLLM evict all of a sequence's blocks at once instead of picking the least recently used blocks like an OS?
options: Every decode step attends over all of the sequence's earlier tokens, so a partially evicted sequence cannot run anyway
GPU memory only supports freeing whole requests
LRU needs timestamps that GPUs cannot record
Partial eviction would break the block size invariant
blocks.explain: Attention reads every previous token's KV, so a sequence with any block missing cannot take its next step. The paper therefore evicts all or none of a sequence's blocks, and gang-schedules sequences that share blocks, such as beam candidates.

lessons.title: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks

blocks.md:
Many requests start with the same tokens: a long system prompt, few-shot examples, a document asked about repeatedly, or the history of a chat. The KV of a token depends only on the tokens before it, so two requests with the same prefix have identical KV for that prefix. Recomputing it is pure waste.

The PagedAttention paper already handled this with prefixes *reserved by the operator in advance*, like shared libraries in an OS. **Automatic prefix caching (APC)** in vLLM does it with no configuration: it keeps the KV blocks of past requests and reuses them whenever a new request starts the same way. Current vLLM turns it on by default for models that support it; `enable_prefix_caching` sets it explicitly.

The key question is how to find a cached block quickly. vLLM gives each **full** block a hash computed from three things: the hash of the previous block (the *parent*), the block's own tokens, and extra keys that make it unique, such as a LoRA adapter ID, image hashes for multimodal inputs, or a cache salt.

blocks.tex: h_0=\mathrm{H}(\varnothing,\ t_{0..B-1},\ e),\qquad h_i=\mathrm{H}(h_{i-1},\ t_{iB..(i+1)B-1},\ e)
blocks.caption: Chaining the parent hash makes block i's hash identify the entire prefix up to the end of block i, not just its own tokens.

blocks.title: Chained block hashes (simplified, block size 4)
blocks.code:
import hashlib

def block_hash(parent, tokens):
    key = repr((parent, tuple(tokens))).encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(key).hexdigest()[:8]

blocks = [["A", "gentle", "breeze", "stirred"],
          ["the", "leaves", "as", "children"],
          ["laughed", "in", "the", "distance"]]
parent = None
for toks in blocks:
    parent = block_hash(parent, toks)
    print(parent)

scenes.caption: Block 0 has no parent, so its hash depends only on its 4 tokens. (vLLM itself hashes token IDs plus extra keys with sha256 by default; this toy hashes the words.)
Block 1's hash mixes in block 0's hash, so it stands for all 8 tokens so far.
Block 2's hash identifies all 12 tokens. A lookup table from hash to physical block now finds any cached prefix one block at a time.

blocks.prompt: Another request is identical except that "children" becomes "kids". Block 2 ("laughed in the distance") has exactly the same tokens as before. Will its block 2 hit the cache?
blocks.reveal:
No. Block 0 still hashes to `d203e4d2` and hits. Block 1 changes to `0a432e57`, and because block 2's hash includes its parent, it becomes `1eb8b515` instead of `09c07380`.

That is the correct behavior: block 2's keys and values were computed while attending to "kids", so they really are different. Matching stops at the first block that differs.

blocks.md: Only **full** blocks are cached. If two prompts share 10 tokens and the block size is 16, nothing is reused. Lookup also always starts from block 0: a shared passage in the middle of two prompts gives no hit, because its KV depends on everything before it.

**Data structures.** All blocks are created up front as a block pool. A *free queue* (a doubly linked list threaded through the blocks) holds every block with reference count 0, in eviction order; a dictionary maps hashes to cached blocks. Freeing a block does **not** erase its KV: it goes to the tail of the free queue still cached. New allocations pop from the head, and if that block is cached, its hash is dropped then. This is LRU eviction.

The example below is the one in the vLLM design docs: block size 4, 10 blocks, rows show owner, reference count, a short form of each cached hash (computed by our toy hash), and the free queue from head to tail.

blocks.title: vLLM block pool with prefix caching (10 blocks, size 4)

scenes.caption: Time 1: request R0 brings 15 prompt tokens. With block size 4 it gets blocks 0 to 3 from the head of the free queue. Blocks 0, 1, 2 are full, so they are hashed and cached; block 3 holds 3 tokens and is not.
Time 2: R0 decodes. Its 16th token fills block 3, which is now hashed and cached; its next token needs a new block, so block 4 is popped from the queue.
Time 3: R1 has 14 prompt tokens, the first 10 equal to R0's. Only blocks 0 and 1 (8 tokens) hit: block 2 matches just 2 of its 4 tokens. Hit blocks get ref 2; R1 computes only 6 tokens.
Time 4: R0 finishes. Blocks 0 and 1 stay in use by R1. Blocks 4, 3, 2 return to the free queue tail in reverse order, still holding their cached KV and hashes.
Time 5: R1 finishes; blocks 6, 5, 1, 0 go to the tail. Every block is free, yet 5 of them still hold reusable KV. Free and cached are not exclusive.
Time 6: R2 (29 tokens, first 12 equal to R0's) hits blocks 0, 1, 2, which are pulled out of the queue. It needs 5 more and pops 7, 8, 9, 4, 3. Block 3 still held R0's cached KV, so it is evicted.

blocks.md: Two details in that trace are deliberate. Hit blocks are *touched* first: their count rises and they leave the free queue, so the allocation that follows cannot evict the very blocks it just matched (blocks 0, 1, 2 at time 6). And a finished request's blocks enter the queue in reverse order, because the last block of a request covers the longest prefix and is the least likely to be reused, so it should be evicted first.

A cache hit needs the whole prefix up to a block boundary to match. Chained hashes make that a sequence of dictionary lookups, and keeping freed blocks cached until they are actually reallocated makes eviction LRU for free.

For multi-tenant servers, vLLM accepts a per-request `cache_salt` that is mixed into the first block's hash, so only requests with the same salt can share blocks. This blocks timing attacks where one user detects another's cached prompt by its faster first token. The default hash is sha256; faster non-cryptographic options exist but raise collision risk.

blocks.question: Block size 16. Request X has a 100-token prompt. Request Y shares X's first 40 tokens, then differs. With X's blocks still cached, how many of Y's prompt tokens are reused?
options: 0, because the prompts differ
blocks.explain: Only full blocks that match from the start are reused. Tokens 0 to 15 and 16 to 31 form two matching full blocks; the third block (32 to 47) contains differing tokens, so its hash differs. 2 x 16 = 32 tokens are reused; the other 8 shared tokens are recomputed.

blocks.question: At time 6 of the trace, why was block 3 evicted while cached block 5 survived?
options: Block 3 had the oldest hash
Block 5 belonged to R1, which has higher priority
Block 3 was nearer the head of the free queue, and allocation pops from the head
Block 5 was full and block 3 was not
blocks.explain: Eviction is just popping the free queue's head. After the hits were removed the queue read 7, 8, 9, 4, 3, 6, 5, and R2 needed 5 blocks, so 3 was the last one taken and its hash was dropped. Block 5 survived only because it sat further back in the queue; age of the hash and owner do not matter.

lessons.title: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays

blocks.md:
SGLang (Zheng et al., 2023) reached the same goal with a different structure. **RadixAttention** keeps the KV of finished requests, both prompts and generated outputs, in a **radix tree**: a trie whose edges can be labeled with whole token sequences rather than single tokens. Each path from the root spells a cached prefix, and the KV tensors live in a paged pool; in the paper the page size is one token.

A new request walks the tree to find its longest cached prefix, reuses that KV, and inserts the rest as new nodes, splitting an edge when it diverges halfway along it.

blocks.title: A radix tree of cached prefixes evolving over time

scenes.caption: The tree starts empty: nothing is cached.
Chat session 1 sends a system prompt and "Hello!"; the model replies "Hi!". Prompt and output are stored as one edge, one node.
Session 1's second turn starts with the whole first turn, which matches the cached node and is reused. Only the new turn is computed and added as a child.
Session 2 shares only the system prompt. The edge is split at the divergence point so both sessions share the system prompt node.
Memory fills up. The least recently used leaf is evicted first, here session 1's second turn. Ancestors stay reusable until they become leaves themselves.
A few-shot query shares no prefix with anything cached, so it becomes a new child of the root.
A second query with the same examples arrives: the node splits so the examples are shared. While both run, the shared node's reference count is 2 and it cannot be evicted.

blocks.md: As in vLLM, every node has a reference count of running requests and only nodes with count 0 can be evicted. SGLang does not set aside a separate cache region: cached tokens and running requests share one pool, and when enough requests are waiting, the cache shrinks to make room for a bigger batch. The paper measured the tree bookkeeping at 0.2 s out of a 74.3 s run with no reuse at all (under 0.3%), so it is on by default.

blocks.tex: \text{cache hit rate}=\frac{\text{number of cached prompt tokens}}{\text{number of prompt tokens}}
blocks.caption: SGLang's definition. It is what the scheduler tries to maximize.

blocks.md: **Cache-aware scheduling.** The order in which waiting requests run changes the hit rate. Switching back and forth between unrelated prefixes makes them evict each other (thrashing). SGLang sorts waiting requests by matched prefix length, longest first, instead of first come, first served. The paper proves that for a batch of requests, visiting the radix tree in depth-first order gives the optimal hit rate when the cache holds at least the longest request, and that longest-shared-prefix-first is equivalent to that order.

blocks.title: Toy simulation: scheduling order vs prefix hit rate

scenes.caption: Simplified simulation: 8 requests, two groups each sharing a 100-token prefix plus 20 unique tokens, arriving A, B, A, B. With room for only one prefix, FCFS thrashes to 0%; grouping by prefix gets 62.5%.
With room for both prefixes, order no longer matters: 6 of 8 requests reuse 100 of 120 tokens either way (600 / 960 = 62.5%, the most possible here). Scheduling matters when the cache is tight.

blocks.md: Longest-prefix-first can starve a request whose prefix is never cached, since others keep jumping ahead. The SGLang paper says so and leaves fair scheduling as future work.

**Hash table or tree?** Both find the longest cached prefix and both evict LRU with reference counts. vLLM's chained hashes work at block granularity and only cache full blocks; the radix tree in the SGLang paper uses a page size of one token, so a shared prefix is reused right up to the token where it diverges. vLLM's docs note that most open-source engines and many public API endpoints now use some form of prefix caching.

**When does it pay?** Caching skips *prefill* for the matched tokens, which lowers time to first token (TTFT) and frees compute. It does nothing for *decode*: each new token still takes one forward pass. vLLM's docs list long-document question answering and multi-turn chat as big wins, and long answers or prompts with nothing in common as cases with no gain.

blocks.title: Request time vs prefix hit rate (illustrative cost model)

scenes.caption: Simplified model with made-up per-token costs (real prefill cost is not exactly linear). A 4000-token prompt with a 200-token answer: total goes from 5.0 s to 4.1 s at 90% hits. TTFT drops 10x; total only modestly.
Long document, short answer (16000 in, 50 out): prefill dominates, and a 90% hit rate cuts the request from 5.0 s to 1.4 s.
Long answers (1000 out): decode dominates, so even 90% hits only move 21.0 s to 20.1 s. This is the limit the vLLM docs warn about.

blocks.md: Prefix caching never changes outputs. It reuses KV for exactly the same tokens instead of recomputing it, so its effects are on speed and memory (outputs can differ only by the tiny floating-point noise any change in batching causes). It helps exactly as much as prefill dominates the work and prefixes repeat.

blocks.question: Which workload benefits least from prefix caching?
options: A support bot whose 3000-token system prompt is identical for every user
Multi-turn chat where each turn resends the full history
Story generation with short, unique prompts and 2000-token outputs
Many questions asked about the same uploaded report
blocks.explain: Caching only skips prefill for repeated prefixes. Unique short prompts give few hits, and with 2000-token outputs nearly all time is decode, which caching does not touch. The other three resend long identical prefixes.

blocks.question: Why does RadixAttention evict leaves before inner nodes?
options: An inner node is a prefix of every node below it, so evicting it first would make its cached descendants unreachable while their KV still occupies memory
Leaves are always the largest nodes
Inner nodes are stored on the CPU
Leaves always have a nonzero reference count
blocks.explain: A cached suffix is only usable together with its whole prefix. Evicting from the leaves up keeps every remaining node reachable, so shared ancestors such as a system prompt survive as long as anything below them is still cached or they are still in use.

blocks.question: You run a multi-tenant API on vLLM and worry that a user could tell whether a competitor recently sent a given prompt. What does vLLM provide for this?
options: Disable PagedAttention
Set the block size to 1
Switch the hash to xxhash
A per-request cache salt mixed into the first block's hash, so only requests with the same salt share cache
blocks.explain: A shared cache leaks information through time to first token. With `cache_salt`, blocks are only shared within a trust group. A faster non-cryptographic hash like xxhash raises collision risk, which the docs warn can leak data in multi-tenant setups.
